questions.q: What does an asset transfer change?
options: The asset's cost and depreciation method
The asset's category
The asset's location, assignment, and/or distribution, without changing cost or category
The asset's useful life
questions.explain: A transfer moves an asset physically or organizationally — location, assignment, or distribution — without touching its cost, category, method, or life.

questions.q: What does a distribution transfer specifically change?
options: The physical building the asset sits in
The employee assigned custody of the asset
Which cost center or expense account bears the asset's depreciation expense
The asset's depreciation method
questions.explain: A distribution transfer changes which part of the organization is charged for the asset's depreciation expense, independent of where it physically sits.

questions.q: Can a transfer apply to only part of an asset rather than the whole thing?
options: No, transfers always apply to 100% of an asset
Yes, a transfer can apply to one specific distribution if the asset is split across multiple cost centers
No, partial transfers are only possible during retirement
Yes, but only for assets still in CIP status
questions.explain: Since an asset can be split across multiple distributions, a transfer can move just one distribution's allocation rather than the entire asset.

questions.q: Why does recording a transfer promptly matter beyond simple bookkeeping accuracy?
options: It has no real business impact beyond internal recordkeeping
It keeps location data accurate for property tax reporting and physical inventory audits
It is required before an asset can be added
It automatically increases the asset's useful life
questions.explain: Accurate, promptly recorded location data is what property tax filings and physical inventory audits rely on; an unrecorded transfer breaks that accuracy.

questions.q: A CNC machine moves plants, gets a new supervisor, and its expense shifts to a new cost center. Is this a reclassification?
options: Yes, because multiple things about the asset changed
No, because its category and cost are unchanged — this is a combination of transfer types
Yes, because the asset's life also changed
No, because transfers are not allowed to combine more than one type
questions.explain: Reclassification specifically means a category change; since this asset's category and cost stay the same, it's a combination of location, assignment, and distribution transfers, not a reclassification.
